doc.title: Bernie Kirsh interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, August 27, 2022

title: Miking a Steinway grand
summary: His two-mic approach to a Steinway and judging stereo image,

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Is there a Bernie Kirsh method of recording a Steinway Grand?

Well, you know yeah I guess you’ve got to figure out, usually I mean you can use more than two, I usually just use two mics and put them in an area that I find apropos to the music we’re going to be recording. And then go in and listen and handle things, maybe adjust things. I mean there’s no tricks. I mean you just put the microphones there and go maybe I should move — am I hearing the left hand far enough to the left? I’ll move the mic. Let’s see does the piano sound like it’s leaning this way? Oh I see. And just listening and changing.
Does it sound like it’s leaning this way?

Yeah. Because if the right hand of the piano — if you’re listening in a stereo image if the right hand of the piano is now moving, sounding like it’s moving toward the center although the note seems to be up further that way on the piano, then to me it’s leaning.
I like that. I’m picturing today’s hopeful engineer who goes to a four year school to get a degree and I wonder if anybody ever says that to them?
Yeah, I don’t know. Good question. I think it just comes out of — you know you record it and you have an idea of what you want it to sound like and if it doesn’t sound like that it’s leaning I guess.
